Community Care Centres (CCCs) are small facilities, with a maximum of 10 beds, located within communities and operated by community health workers. These centres provide isolation for Ebola patients to prevent further transmission of the virus within households and communities. Additionally, CCCs offer basic curative and palliative care in an environment supported by the patient’s family and community. This approach respects local traditions and is part of a broader community-based strategy to combat Ebola. The community approach includes four key pillars of the Ebola response strategy: As a new approach in the Ebola response, CCCs require evaluation, and the WHO recommends conducting a lessons learned exercise after implementing pilot centres. Validating the concept will allow for larger-scale implementation. Key considerations for CCC implementation include community engagement and empowerment, involving communities in planning, implementation, and operation. CCCs are small structures where Ebola patients can be housed separately from their families and communities. These centres are equipped with appropriate water, sanitation, waste management, and disinfection facilities. A triage protocol is applied to assess patients' risk of having Ebola before entry, and suspected and confirmed cases are housed separately. Patients with wet symptoms (e.g., vomiting, bleeding, diarrhea), who are more contagious, are separated from those without such symptoms. The design and care processes aim to minimize transmission risks. Patients in CCCs receive respectful, compassionate care 24/7 from trained community members or health staff. At a minimum, care includes food, water, oral rehydration, presumptive malaria treatment (where appropriate), antipyretics, analgesics, and broad-spectrum oral antibiotics under medical supervision. Intravenous fluids are administered when supplies and trained staff are available. Psychosocial support is provided for patients and their families, along with community awareness initiatives. Family kits for patients and deceased individuals’ families are also distributed. Staffing at CCCs includes caregivers, cleaners, communicators, and security personnel as needed. All staff are trained in Ebola management and infection prevention and control (IPC) and are supervised daily. A supervision team regularly visits CCCs to mentor health workers, educate the community, collect samples for laboratory confirmation, and assess safety and adherence to standards. CCCs complement existing Ebola Treatment Units (ETUs) by addressing geographical and capacity challenges. Many ETUs have exceeded their capacity, leaving infected patients in their homes, which increases the risk of transmission. CCCs provide a rapid and localized option for isolation and care, particularly in new transmission hotspots. Community care allows patients to receive care close to home, often from members of their own community, making the experience more reassuring and comfortable. Some communities have already begun building their own centres, demonstrating a willingness to actively respond to the outbreak. Home-based care, while an option in some contexts, poses significant risks of Ebola transmission to household members and the community. It is unrealistic to expect households in confined environments to adequately protect themselves from infection at all times. Without active mentoring, medical supervision, PPE supply chains, decentralized laboratory testing, waste management, and safe burial procedures, home-based care is likely to increase community transmission. Properly implemented CCCs can slow the progression of the epidemic by reducing community contact with infected individuals and providing care close to patients’ homes. This approach improves community acceptance and reduces the need to transport infectious patients, which has sometimes led to infections among taxi and ambulance drivers. Modeling studies suggest that CCCs could reduce the basic reproduction number (R0) below 1 if the time from symptom onset to admission is sufficiently shortened. An R0 below 1 indicates a slowing of transmission and an eventual end to the epidemic. CCCs will not open if there are doubts about the safety and security of staff and patients. Efforts are made to avoid diverting staff or supplies from other health facilities. If necessary, supply production can be accelerated, and countries should allocate resources appropriately. CCCs are not intended to replace ETUs but rather to complement them as part of a comprehensive community approach to reduce transmission risks. Some countries, such as Liberia and Sierra Leone, have chosen not to allow family members inside CCCs. Instead, alternative solutions, such as transparent walls or mobile phones for communication, can be implemented. Open communication with the community is crucial, and families should be kept informed about CCC activities and the condition of their loved ones. If communities allow family members to care for patients, only one designated caregiver should be permitted to reduce household transmission risks.
